rules.because: No archetype scored above the floor, so docdna will not guess what kind of system this is.
This system authenticates people, which means it has a boundary worth attacking and nothing describes it.
A pipeline pushes this to a running environment and the path it takes is written only in YAML.
This repository has release tags and no file that says what changed between them.
People install this and see it, so what changed and who can use it are the two questions they will ask.
Strangers pay to keep their data in this system and every one of them will eventually ask how it is protected.
No compliance program exists in this repository and no external reviewer has been confirmed, so there is no attestation package to assemble.
A compliance workspace is wired into this repository and it will ask for evidence on a schedule.
This code owns a persistent schema and the meaning of its columns lives nowhere but in the columns.
Downstream consumers read these tables and a silent schema change breaks work nobody in this repository can see.
An actively changed codebase with more than one author and no recorded decisions relitigates the same choices every quarter.
At least one committed document is older than the source file it describes.
Firmware in the field can only be fixed by people who know which build is on the device.
No model inference, model SDK, training stack, or retrieval pipeline exists here, so the EU AI instruments do not apply.
No user is in the EU or EEA and no public-sector authorizer has been confirmed, so EU market instruments do not apply.
This repository publishes no software artifact and contains no firmware, so there is no shipped product for an EU conformity file.
No coding-agent context files exist here, so there are no host rules to extend.
Nothing in this repository defines an alert or an on-call rotation, so there is no page for a runbook to answer.
Nothing here declares, migrates, or maps a data store, so there is no data to classify or restore.
This repository declares no third-party dependencies, so a bill of materials would list nothing.
Nothing in this repository deploys anywhere and no operator was named, so there is no production to run.
No feature flag system is configured here, so there is no live flag set to register.
This code exposes no network interface, so there is no contract for another program to depend on.
Nothing here is tagged, versioned, or published, so there is no release for notes to describe.
No scanner runs against this code, so there are no findings for an evidence index to collect.
There is no authentication, no server, and no stored data here, so there is no trust boundary to model.
This system has no human-facing interface, so there is nothing for an accessibility test to exercise.
Feature flags change production behaviour and nothing here records which ones are still live.
No health data library or health record vocabulary appears in this repository, so the HIPAA-specific rows do not apply.
This deploys to somewhere real, so how it gets there and what to do when it breaks are load-bearing.
An MCP server is driven by programs, and a tool schema nobody wrote down becomes somebody else's outage.
Schema migrations run against data that has to survive them, forwards and backwards.
Three or more independently deployable units mean the boundaries between them are now the design.
No model SDK, training stack, or prompt file appears in this repository, so the AI obligations did not fire.
An on-call rotation is configured and the escalation path it pages into is not written down anywhere.
Strangers depend on this package's public surface and have no other way to learn it.
A skill is installed into hosts its author does not control and fired by prompts its author did not write.
Model behaviour changes without a code change, so the test strategy has to cover evaluation and not just units.
Store review asks what data leaves the device, and the answer has to exist before the submission does.
A health data standard is a dependency here, and health records have a different retention answer than everything else.
Health data indicators surface the HIPAA legal instruments for confirmation without treating repository evidence as a legal verdict.
The people who run this in production did not write it and cannot read the authors' minds at three in the morning.
Card data crosses this system and the flow has to be drawn before anyone can argue about its scope.
Payment indicators surface the PCI validation instruments for confirmation without treating repository evidence as a legal verdict.
A public interface has users who cannot ask the authors what changed or why they cannot use it.
An external authorizer decides whether this ships and they read evidence, not source.
A functional safety standard is referenced here and docdna does not carry the assurance case document set.
Something leaves this repository as a binary and lands on a machine the authors will never see.
Both files are owned by repo-ready, so docdna records a pointer row instead of writing over them.
A document that goes unmaintained turns into confident fiction, and these are the ones no later run can regenerate.
No payment processor integration or cardholder data vocabulary appears in this repository, so the PCI-specific rows do not apply.
Personal data sits on an entity this code treats as a person, and how long it is kept is currently undocumented.
Anyone can create an account here, which makes every change a change to somebody else's day.
This repository declares a publishable package and docdna cannot see whether anyone outside the authors installs it.
Paying users depend on this working and on being told before it changes under them.
Nobody outside the team that writes this uses it, so these documents have no reader.
Another team integrates against this and cannot read the authors' intentions out of the source.
Anyone can use this, and anyone includes the person who finds the vulnerability.
Something deploys this automatically and nothing in the repository says who answers when it breaks.
The customer installs and runs this themselves, so every operational assumption has to survive leaving the building.
A team that did not write this gets paged for it and has to act without the authors.
Compliance program files exist, so a person must identify whether they support an auditor, customer review, regulator, or internal program.
Government of Canada signals appear in this repository and docdna will not decide on its own whether a government buyer is in the loop.
Health data indicators are present, but only a person can confirm whether the organisation is a HIPAA covered entity or business associate.
Payment indicators are present, but only a person can confirm whether the organisation is a PCI merchant or service provider.
United States federal program vocabulary appears here and a hint may open this question but may never answer it.
An auditor samples evidence on a schedule and evidence that was never written is a finding.
An external authorizer signs before this ships, and what they sign is evidence rather than working software.
A confirmed customer security review commonly asks for independent testing and a recorded security design review.
A customer security questionnaire asks for these by name and a slow answer costs the deal.
A confirmed government authorization requires implemented controls to be mapped to reviewable technical evidence.
A confirmed government authorizer requires the authorization, assessment, impact, and attestation instruments it will sign or accept.
A person confirmed that this organisation is a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, so its risk, agreement, inventory, and training evidence is required.
The confirmed HIPAA relationship requires access, audit, incident, identity, and notice safeguards around protected health information.
No external body audits, certifies, or authorizes this before it ships, and no compliance workspace exists in the repository.
A person confirmed a PCI merchant or service provider relationship, so the cardholder flow and its access, hardening, key, and audit controls are required.
The confirmed PCI relationship requires a human-owned validation instrument and independent penetration-test evidence.
A confirmed sector regulator requires human-owned impact, testing, design-review, and training evidence before release.
A person confirmed an auditor relationship, so the system description and the human-owned testing, review, and training records are required evidence.
The confirmed auditor relationship requires durable access, change, incident, supplier, and cloud-control evidence across the review period.
This system helps decide something that changes a person's money, job, or legal standing, and that person is entitled to know how.
Model output and personal records meet inside this system, and no signal is allowed to say what that output is used for.
This code stores personal data on entities it treats as people, and only a human may say whether it decides anything about them.
Automated decisions about staff are still decisions about people, and staff can ask how they were made.
EU AI Act vocabulary appears alongside real inference calls, and the market answer decides whether any of it applies.
European Union signals appear in this repository, and a hint may open this question but may never set a verdict.
A user interface confirmed for the EU market or public-sector authorization requires signed accessibility and conformance instruments.
A person confirmed EU or EEA users for a detected AI system, so its Annex IV technical documentation is required.
A person confirmed EU or EEA users for shipped software, so the CRA technical file and declaration of conformity are required.
A person confirmed EU or EEA users for a repository that trains models, so the GPAI provider documentation is required.
Users sitting in the EU bring obligations that attach to their data on the day it is collected.
A person confirmed EU or EEA users and personal data is present, so the processing, notice, subprocessor, and retention records are required.
A person confirmed EU or EEA users and special-category data is present, so a human-owned impact screening is required.
Every user of this system sits inside the organization that builds it and no external body reviews it.
Canadian and United States privacy statutes attach to consumer personal data regardless of how small the company is.
A day of downtime is an inconvenience here and nobody is paged when it happens.
Minutes of downtime cost money or safety here, and the recovery path has to exist before the minute it is needed.
Nobody will maintain these after today, so docdna writes what a later run can regenerate and refuses the rest.
A team has agreed to keep these documents true, so which part of it owns which document has to be written down.
The documentation of record lives outside this repository, so these rows are tracked as present elsewhere rather than missing.
I only see documentation committed to this repository.
This artifact is run to reproduce a result, not operated as a service, and no deployment target exists in the tree.
A result nobody else can re-run is a claim, not a finding.
Alert rules fire into a repository that documents no response to any of them.
This pipeline ships a build made mostly of other people's code and nothing records what went into it.
A credential-shaped literal is sitting in a tracked file in this repository.
One author and a small commit history: the decisions in this repository still fit in one person's head.
Nothing external governs this repository and there is no second person for a process document to align.
One author has committed here in the last year, so there is nobody to onboard and no release ritual to hand over.
A single-author utility this small is specified by its own source, and a parallel spec would rot before anyone read it.
This tool has one user who is also its author, so its interface needs no reference page.
Documents in this repository have not been touched since the code they describe moved on.
Published artifact with no private disclosure route.
Data lands in an analytical store here and nothing states what it is or when it gets deleted.
A weak hash is called in application code and nothing records whether that choice was deliberate.
